title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Becomes Second-Fastest Movie to Hit $1 Billion Overseas, Powers to $1.67 Billion Globally
description:
Spidey keeps climbing… and climbing… and climbing at the box office.

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has amassed a heroic $1.67 billion after just 12
body:
Spidey keeps climbing… and climbing… and climbing at the box office.

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has amassed a heroic $1.67 billion after just 12 days in theaters, including $1.01 billion internationally and $655 million domestically. It’s the second-fastest movie to reach the billion-dollar mark overseas, behind only 2019’s comic book behemoth “Avengers: Endgame.” Among its numerous milestones, “Brand New Day” has already become the biggest movie of the year as well as the 12th-highest-grossing release of all time. It’s a testament to the enduring popularity of Peter Parker, as well as the pent-up demand for Tom Holland’s fourth solo adventure as Marvel’s web-slinging hero. After all, audiences hadn’t seen Spider-Man on the big screen since 2021’s blockbuster “No Way Home.”
	

	In its second weekend of release, “Spider-Man” collected $236 million overseas and $145 million domestically. Most films would be lucky to earn that much in their debuts, much less after an entire week in theaters. China remains the largest international market with $29.1 million over the weekend and $186.7 million to date, followed by the United Kingdom with $16 million over the weekend and $87.4 million to date, as well as Mexico with $15.3 million over the weekend and $65.8 million to date.


	With repeat viewings from comic book fans and without much in the way of competition, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is poised to dominate throughout the rest of the summer and into the fall. Sony’s tentpole is barreling toward $2 billion worldwide, a benchmark that only seven films in history — “Avatar,” “Avengers: Endgame” and “Titanic” among them — have ever achieved. At this breakneck pace, box office watchers are hard-pressed to predict where ticket sales will ultimately wind up.
	

	Meanwhile, “The Odyssey” has remained a force, even with the outsized appeal of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.” Christopher Nolan’s Greek epic earned $79 million overseas in its fourth weekend of release, as well as $31.5 million in North America. With $1.104 billion globally, “The Odyssey” officially ranks as Nolan’s highest-grossing movie of all time, overtaking 2012’s “The Dark Knight Rises” ($1.08 billion) and 2009’s “The Dark Knight” ($1.008 billion). It’s also the biggest release ever for Imax with $289 million, surpassing the tally of “Avatar” with $271 million. 

	Also this weekend, Paramount’s animated “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie” opened to $23 million from 30 overseas markets, representing 75% of the international footprint. Top territories were China with $5.5 million, France with $4.5 million and the U.K. with $2.2 million. The third theatrical feature based on the animated kids’ series is opening next weekend in North America and 22 additional markets.

title: Box Office: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Flies to Third-Biggest Second Weekend of All Time With $145 Million
description: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is continuing its unparalleled box office run, scoring another $145 million domestically during its second weekend in th
body:
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is continuing its unparalleled box office run, scoring another $145 million domestically during its second weekend in theaters.

	Just to put those stratospheric ticket sales in context, only one movie this year — “Toy Story 5” — earned around that much in its opening weekend, with Disney’s Pixar adventure debuting to $159 million. “Brand New Day” scored the third-biggest second weekend of all time, trailing just 2015’s “Star Wars: The Force Awakens” with $149 million and 2019’s “Avengers: Endgame” with $147 million. Only eight movies have ever surpassed $100 million in their sophomore outings. 
	

	After opening to a record-setting $355 million domestically and heroic $932 million globally, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has now generated a staggering $655 million in North America and $1.67 billion globally. Sony and Marvel’s web-slinging adventure, starring Tom Holland as the title hero, flew past the billion-dollar mark in just six days and is barreling toward $2 billion. At this pace, box office watchers are wondering whether “Spidey” has the staying power to become the first movie to ever reach $1 billion at the domestic box office and become the sole film to hit $3 billion globally. “The Force Awakens” is currently the highest-grossing release in domestic box office history with $936.6 million, while 2009’s “Avatar” and “Avengers: Endgame” stand as the biggest movies worldwide with $2.9 billion and $2.7 billion, respectively, after several re-releases.


	In a distant second place on domestic box office charts, “The Odyssey” remained muscular with $31.5 million in its fourth weekend of release — a 38% decline. With $461 million domestically and $1.1 billion worldwide, “The Odyssey” officially ranks as Christopher Nolan’s highest-grossing movie of all time, overtaking 2012’s “The Dark Knight Rises” ($1.08 billion) and 2009’s “The Dark Knight” ($1.008 billion) to notch the achievement. 
	

	Nolan’s Greek epic, starring Matt Damon, isn’t close to slowing down in theaters. Imax screens are sold out through mid-September, with the format already contributing a massive $289 million in ticket sales. This weekend, “The Odyssey” became Imax’s highest-grossing release of all time, surpassing the lifetime haul of “Avatar” with $271 million. And the film doesn’t even open in China, the world’s second-biggest moviegoing market, until next week. It’s a testament to Nolan’s bankability that a nearly three-hour, adult-skewing sword-and-sandal adventure, adapted from Homer’s 2,700-year-old poem, is one of this summer’s biggest blockbusters.

	“Christopher Nolan has earned audiences’ trust by consistently delivering must-see theatrical events,” says Jim Orr, Universal’s president of domestic theatrical distribution. “And ‘The Odyssey’ is him operating at the peak of his powers.”

	With “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey” capturing the lion’s share of attention, three new movies opened nationwide to mostly disappointing results. 

	Universal’s raucous romantic comedy “One Night Only” debuted below expectations with $5.7 million from 3,012 theaters, enough for third place on box office charts. Callum Turner and Monica Barbaro star in the R-rated movie, which revolves around two strangers who keep running into each other around a dystopian New York City on the one night a year when premarital sex is legal. Opening weekend crowds were mostly female (70%), while more than half of ticket buyers were between the ages of 18 and 34. Director Will Gluck’s prior film, 2023’s “Anyone But You,” starring Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell, opened to $6 million. However, that movie, which opened around Christmastime, became a sleeper hit with $88 million domestically and $220 million globally by the end of its run. “One Night Only” scored a decent “B+” grade on CinemaScore exit polls, so Universal is hoping the $25 million-budgeted movie can enjoy a similarly long life on the big screen.

	“Super Troopers 3” launched at No. 4 with $4 million from 2,760 venues, by far the lowest start in the comedy trilogy. The original 2001 adventure, following the over-the-top antics of a ragtag group of New England highway patrol officers, opened to $6.2 million, not adjusted for inflation, while the 2018 sequel captured $15.1 million in its debut. Critics and audiences were mixed on the hijinks of Broken Lizard, the comedy troupe at the center of these movies, with “Super Trooper 3” landing a “B-” grade on CinemaScore and 48% on Rotten Tomatoes.
	

	Director Eli Roth’s slasher “Ice Cream Man” scraped together $2 million from 1,671 screens in its opening weekend, landing in eighth place behind holdovers like “Toy Story 5,” “Minions & Monsters” and “Moana.” Roth, who directed “Borderlands” after making a name for himself with gory thrillers like “Hostel” and “The Green Inferno,” raised the $5.5 million needed to fund “Ice Cream Man” and self-distributed the movie through his indie company The Horror Section. 

	Meanwhile, three indie releases — A24’s coming-of-age story “Tony,” Mubi’s slasher “Teenage Sex and Death and Camp Miasma” and Magnolia’s New York-set drama “Late Fame” — each managed to impress while playing on just a few screens.

	“Tony,” a biopic about the origins of celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain, served up one of the best screen averages of the year with $348,955 from six screens in New York City and Los Angeles — translating to $58,159 per location. A24 is behind the other top screen averages of 2026, including the Charli XCX mockumentary “The Moment” ($107,000 per screen) and Olivia Wilde’s relationship drama “The Invite ($54,158 per screen). Those metrics don’t always result in populist hits. “The Moment” fizzled with $5 million globally, while “The Invite” has earned a solid $42 million and counting. “Tony,” directed by Matt Johnson and starring “The Holdovers” breakout Dominic Sessa as a young Bourdain, has been positively reviewed, though its commercial appeal will be tested as A24 continues to roll out the movie in select markets before bringing it nationwide on Aug. 21.

	“Teenage Sex and Death and Camp Miasma,” the latest from “I Saw the TV Glow” director Jane Schoenbrun, earned $251,000 from five screens — averaging $50,300 per location. Nearly 80% of audiences were under 35, while half were under 25 years old, according to exit polls. The well-reviewed movie revolves around a filmmaker (Hannah Einbinder) who is hired to direct a reboot of a slasher franchise. Mubi will open the film, co-starring Gillian Anderson, in 50 new theaters next weekend before launching nationwide on Aug. 21.

	“Late Fame,” which is screening at just two theaters, New York’s Film Forum and Film at Lincoln Center, brought in $38,000 or $19,000 per venue. Directed by Kent Jones, “Late Fame” follows Willem Dafoe as a former poet who befriends a group of young artists.
	

	Next weekend will bring a handful of new wide releases, including the Warner Bros. sci-fi mystery “The End of Oak Street” with Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, Paramount’s “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie” and Black Bear’s “The Rivals of Amziah King” starring Matthew McConaughey. However, those movies won’t be able to catch Spidey at the top of the box office charts.

title: ‘Our Time Will Come’ Review: Two Orphans Journey to Accra to Find Their Kin in an Emotionally Absorbing Ghanaian Drama
description: Elements of “Oliver Twist” are given a West African update in “Our Time Will Come,” an atmospheric and emotionally absorbing feature debut from writ
body:
Elements of “Oliver Twist” are given a West African update in “Our Time Will Come,” an atmospheric and emotionally absorbing feature debut from writer-director Amartei Armar, who thankfully cares too much for his orphaned characters to torture them (and us) with unending miserabilism.  Beginning as a road trip, then shifting to a punishing vision of hardscrabble life in Accra, the film blossoms into a story of irrevocable bonds forged out of shared adversity. Handsomely shot by John Kwame Markin and anchored by an adult-sized performance from teen Idrissu Tontie Jr., “Our Time Will Come” (presented in Marrakech’s 2025 Atlas Workshops as “Vagabonds”) plays with certain narrative conventions in such distinctive ways that it’s likely to find a welcoming home wherever it travels following its Locarno premiere.
	

	Armar’s Ghana is one where family ties have been eroded and ethnic identity precludes any notion of national solidarity. Within the vacuum left by rural flight and grinding poverty, people’s instincts are to rebuff anyone resembling the outsider they used to be themselves, making for a dog-eat-dog world where protection is possible only if a self-described family welcomes the newcomer into their midst. Oblivion is just one step away, and kinship, whether by blood or affinity, is redefined for a modern world in which traditional safety nets have been rent asunder.


	The bond between 15-year-old Owusu (Tontie Jr.) and seven-year-old Adobea (Dorothy Adobea Tandoh) is that of brother and sister: Owusu’s mother left him in the care of a friend and disappeared, but that friend died when giving birth to Adobea. We don’t know why the two kids decide to flee their orphanage, but Owusu’s selfless protection of his young charge has such potent resonance that the wisdom of their escape is never questioned, despite learning that Adobea suffers from the same blood disease as her mother.
	

	Their goal is to reach Accra and locate Owusu’s long-lost mother: “If we can find her in Accra, we can be a family again,” he tells Adobea, though the only physical evidence he has is an old photograph. Owusu keeps them moving as if compelled by instinct, driven to find water, a place to sleep, and a kind person willing to give them a lift. By shooting these early scenes outside in full daylight, with plenty of space, Armar sets up a stark contrast between the light-filled openness of the countryside — not without its dangers — and the dark, crowded, disorienting city where the youngsters are heading.

	An open-air market seems like the best place to show his mother’s photo and ask people if they know her, but these two weary, dirty provincials speaking a different language are clear targets for any scam, and all their stuff is nicked by Obolo (O’Bryan Nana Kwame Enyan), a scrappy street kid with an eye patch. In desperation Owusu searches for the thief, threading through the slums and finding him in an abandoned building with a small band of youths led by the charismatic Ziggy (Emmanuel Wilberforce), a sort of Artful Dodger who tests the newcomer and then, assured of his mettle, welcomes him and Adobea to the “family.”

	Up until that moment, the abuse (and fear of abuse) experienced by Owusu and Adobae threatens to become relentless, but Ziggy’s protection marks a shift, not so much in their fortunes but their ability to survive without constant fear of violence. Suga (Barbara Yong-Jin), the one girl in the group, drops her insolent, mocking demeanor to become nurturing towards Adobea, and everyone contributes to the group’s survival by hawking and transporting anything that’s sellable.

	The film’s pointed critique of a fractured society severely damaged by playing catch-up capitalism is unmistakable, but for those familiar with recent Ghanaian politics, Armar’s poignant assessment goes deeper. Not by chance does he include a billboard emblazoned with “#ReadTheBill,” part of a campaign among activists designed to raise awareness of a 2024 so-called “Family Values” bill crafted to criminalize the LGBTQ+ community (it passed); instead of supporting alternate families at a moment when the disconnect between traditional notions of blood ties and the actual state of kinship units has never been more cavernous, the government chose a red flag issue rather than addressing the country’s real problems. While such knowledge isn’t needed to appreciate “Our Day Will Come,” the quietly inserted political angle makes clear that Armar intends his film as much for his home country as international festival audiences.
	

	Whatever background audiences bring to the table, there’s no mistaking the director’s deeply effective working relationship with Idrissu Tontie Jr., who also appeared in some of Armar’s previous shorts and unmistakably holds the film with his impressive shift from tense, driven protector to relaxed, swaggering urban denizen. In fact, the charismatic cast all shine, as does Kwame Markin’s camerawork, nicely attuned to the differing emotional registers demanded by location and mood. However, Armar inserts three music montages, presumably to keep the energy going, when one would have sufficed.

title: Naseeruddin Shah, Gurvinder Singh Turn a Village’s Real Grief Into Locarno Competition Title ‘Rehmat’: ‘It’s Important That These Films Get Made’
description: The family living in the house that “Rehmat” uses as Rashid Ali’s ancestral home lost a son to a drug overdose shortly after Indian filmmaker Gurvin
body:
The family living in the house that “Rehmat” uses as Rashid Ali’s ancestral home lost a son to a drug overdose shortly after Indian filmmaker Gurvinder Singh and his crew first met them. 

	Singh tells Variety, “The actual family that lives there lost their 19-year-old son after we met them for the first time. When I looked at him, the first thought that ran in my mind was that he was on drugs. And he died of an overdose within two months. What else do I need to say? How can that not affect you as a filmmaker planning a film in that scenario. How can you avoid depicting such a state of affairs?”
	

	“Rehmat” has its world premiere in the Concorso Internazionale, the main competition of the 79th Locarno Film Festival. It is the only Indian feature in the section this year and will compete for the festival’s top honor, the Pardo d’Oro. 


	Adapted from short stories by the Punjabi writer Ajeet Cour, “Rehmat” weaves three narratives set in present-day Punjab around themes of displacement and inherited grief. Singh says the material resonated with him directly through family history. “She has written about many themes, uprootedness being one of them, and she belongs to my grandparents’ generation that migrated from Lahore or other parts of west Punjab to Delhi,” he says. “That was the sort of affinity I had with her stories.”

	Three decades after he began documenting Punjab’s folk ballads and oral histories, and 15 years after his debut feature “Anhey Ghorhey Da Daan” premiered in Venice, Singh says the film has given him something he didn’t expect. “I never experienced the Partition, but did feel a sense of trauma during the years of militancy and the anti-Sikh carnage in Delhi in 1984,” he says. “Frankly speaking, this film offers me a closure. I feel it has brought out all that I needed to express about the divided land and its people.”
	

	The film stars revered Indian thespian Naseeruddin Shah as Rashid Ali, a Punjabi Muslim man whose family left before Partition and who returns to his birthplace after a lifetime in England. Shah says he committed to the role before knowing any of its specifics. “I’d seen and been deeply moved by Gurvinder’s films,” Shah tells Variety. “His cinematic sensibility and his take on the turmoil in his home state made profound statements. I just thought I’d like to be part of such films.”

	That leap of faith went both ways. Singh says, “I approached Naseer without having written the script, only having a vague outline of the character of Rashid in my mind. His acceptance gave me the possibilities to expand and flesh it, knowing the kind of conviction, intellect and charisma he will bring into it. The responsibility became a flight of imagination. It was a new territory for me.”

	Of working with Shah on set, Singh says, “I had decided that I would initially observe him in front of the camera and then figure out my approach. But I kept doing that and hardly needed to direct him,” describing how the actor’s “use of the body, gestures, handling of objects” turned Rashid “into his own personal expression.”

	Shah, who is not Punjabi and does not speak the language fluently, says, “I agree I don’t have the Punjabi heartiness and I don’t look Punjabi. But I think that helped to identify Rashid as an outsider. I don’t speak Punjabi fluently but practice helped.” On the ambiguity of a character who initially introduces himself to the village as God, Shah adds: “A character doesn’t have to be understood by the actor playing him. Actors aren’t psychoanalysts. One must be able to empathize with the character’s situation.”

	Singh’s preference for long, unbroken takes runs through the film, including the opening shot that establishes Seema’s world. Singh says, “The sense of uninterrupted time that the long take affords, both with the static and the mobile camera, is highly involving for me as a spectator, and my first instinct is to attempt that. But there are scenes where you know it will not be practical or even desirable, hence the montage has to be employed. Both create a different quality of attention and being. And perhaps life is also like that. Our ways of seeing and engaging keep altering.” 
	

	Shah adds, “I love long takes. It fits beautifully with my stage work. Frankly I don’t believe there’s a great difference between stage and film acting if truth is what you’re looking to find.”

	Beyond the ancestral house, Singh says the village itself, with its crumbling 19th-century school building and untended lanes, reshaped the narrative during location scouting. Asked how he views Punjab today, Singh says, “Bleak from the perspective of lack of imagination among the youth or those of my generation, not because of any lack of compassion. People are sticking to the glory of ownership of land and the caste they belong to. It has given them a false sense of bravado and entitlement. And the gender discourse is abysmal, especially in the villages. No wonder so many young girls are escaping to the West.”

	Alongside Shah, the cast includes Suvinder Vicky, Mita Vashisht, Navjot Randhawa and Diya Kamboj, plus the celebrated Punjabi poet Jaswant Zafar, making his screen acting debut at 60 as Harjap. Of casting Zafar, Singh says, “Whenever I have cast a non-actor in a major role, it is fully knowing that the person will play himself or herself on screen. So Zafar became Harjap for me. He has all the natural qualities I had imagined in Harjap and a profound sense of the feelings that he carries, both as a common man and as an intellectual.”

	“Rehmat” is produced by Singh and Arpana Caur, with Andrei Cosmin Illes and Némésis Srour serving as co-producers. The film is a co-production between India’s Vahao Studio and Paris-based Pavo Films, the outfit Illes and Srour launched earlier this year, with “Rehmat” as its debut project.

	Shah, whose career stretches back to the parallel cinema movement of the 1970s, says, “My early work prepared me for a film like this. I think Gurvinder has surpassed other contemporary filmmakers in India.” Of the film’s Partition-era subject matter, he says, “I believe it’s important that these films get made. Even if not widely seen now, they will remain as a testament.”

	Asked what he’s working on next, Singh says, “I am not sure what I want to do after this. I came to the cinema through some conspiracy of the universe. I grew up painting and writing. I am painting again these days.”

schema.headline: Naseeruddin Shah, Gurvinder Singh Turn a Village’s Real Grief Into Locarno Competition Title ‘Rehmat’: ‘It’s Important That These Films Get Made’

title: ‘Donkey Princess’ Review: A Princess Escapes the Kingdom, but Not the Patriarchy, in an Inventive, Shape-Shifting Fairytale
description: Chilean duo Cristobal León and Joaquín Cociña made a dream nightmare debut with “The Wolf House,” a stop-motion fantasy that turned heads both with
body:
Chilean duo Cristobal León and Joaquín Cociña made a dream nightmare debut with “The Wolf House,” a stop-motion fantasy that turned heads both with its wholly original design — incorporating claymation, puppetry and papier-mâché to palpably handmade but immersively surreal effect — and its trajectory from a seemingly juvenile storybook premise to very grownup recesses of horror and trauma. Their 2024 follow-up “The Hyperboreans” captured fewer imaginations with its dense, narratively abstruse melange of history, psychology and political theory, but still dazzled with technique, adding live-action cinematography to the filmmakers’ varied visual quiltwork. In their beguiling third feature, “Donkey Princess,” León and Cociña split the difference between their first two, continuing their singular exploration of hybrid live-action cinema, but fruitfully returning to adult fairytale terrain.
	

	Premiering in the international competition at Locarno, this is distinctive, aesthetically rich filmmaking that consolidates its helmers’ auteur status, and has the right balance of accessible and avant-garde components to ensure a life beyond the festival circuit — though the substance of its story lingers slightly less in the mind than its remarkable presentation. “Donkey Princess” doesn’t quite match “The Wolf House” for darkly enveloping atmosphere and gnawing emotional impact, but not much does; still, its portrayal of a mythic princess, whose tortured daddy issues follow her even after she’s spirited into the real world, builds to a climax both touching and disquieting.
	

	As suggested by the title, the script (written, like “The Wolf House,” by the directors in collaboration with novelist Alejandra Moffat) riffs on the 17th-century Charles Perrault tale “Donkeyskin” — not one that Disney ever dared touch, giving its discomfiting incest-themed premise, though Jacques Demy gave it delightfully offbeat film treatment in 1970. More downbeat in its whimsy, “Donkey Princess” centers on Princess Diana (“Hyperboreans” star Antonia Giesen), who doesn’t bear any resemblance to her famous British namesake, save for the fact that she’s suffocated by the demands of her very patriarchal kingdom.

	Said kingdom is realized in a mixture of animated imagery and winningly ramshackle production design by Natalia Geisse: toadstool-shaped castle turrets rendered in what looks like cake frosting, fiberglass mountain formations and forests forged from stray, dry branches, accessorized with the odd flurry of 2D cartoon butterflies and birds. (Fans of the directors’ stop-motion interlude in Ari Aster’s “Beau is Afraid” will spot some familiar landscape textures here.) Tinted in queasy shades of turquoise and puce, it does not look like a world made to last, and for Diana, it isn’t. Guarded obsessively by her father (Francisco Melo) since her mother’s untimely death, she yearns for escape from his clutches; when she meets charming commoner Lalo (Andrew Bargsted), she falls swiftly in love, both with him and the prospect of life outside the royal court.

	For the King — who really has taken very badly to widowed life, having outlawed love throughout the land — this will not do. Lalo is swiftly banished to an orange-skied hellscape strewn with thorns and vultures: a witty fusion of silhouette animation and tactile set construction. Before he goes, however, he gives Diana a bracelet said to grant wishes across space and time; in short order, she’s transported to the urban bustle of contemporary Chile. There, she and Lalo live together as parallel versions of themselves, also working alongside each other in the pest control business. If this seems a pretty compromised happily-ever-after, there’s also the fact that her father, too, has been teleported to this new realm: an aging invalid stripped of his powers, but still plenty burdensome.

	That’s not the last dimensional shift in “Donkey Princess,” as Dina is shuffled through various lives and personae, but is never quite free or happy in any of them: The naïve yet despairing time-travel mechanics of Bertrand Bonello’s recent “The Beast” come to mind here, as its various temporal paths do eventually converge into a single, climactic tragedy, with the open-ended possibility of freedom. León and Cociña’s storytelling style can be opaque — the film’s opening salvo, in particular, feels hurried and scrambled — but it gains in grace and clarity, with a concluding shift in register toward near-total realism. That’s the biggest surprise from these most feverishly world-building of filmmakers, even if their most satisfying feature to date remains their most animated one. “Donkey Princess” might lack “The Wolf House’s” intensity of vision and purpose, but it feels an intriguingly transitional work in an oeuvre that could go anywhere from here.

schema.headline: ‘Donkey Princess’ Review: A Princess Escapes the Kingdom, but Not the Patriarchy, in an Inventive, Shape-Shifting Fairytale

title: David Ellison Is Promising Theater Owners Contractual Guarantees for Paramount-Warner Bros. 30-Film Annual Slate. But What if Moviegoers Don’t Care?
description: There’s no question that David Ellison, the doggedly ambitious CEO of Paramount Skydance, loves movies and filmmaking. In making his case for Paramo
body:
There’s no question that David Ellison, the doggedly ambitious CEO of Paramount Skydance, loves movies and filmmaking. In making his case for Paramount’s eye-poppingly pricey megadeal to merge with Warner Bros., he has repeatedly pledged that the combined company will release a lot more movies — to the tune of at least 30 titles per year in theaters.

	When Ellison launched his hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, before he beat out Netflix to clinch a deal, he planted a flag with a pledge that the merged entity would pump more than 30 titles into theaters with “traditional” windows. And ever since, he’s been waving the 30-film number around like a magic wand that will save the movie business.
	

	Ellison is now offering three-year contractually enforceable commitments to the U.S.’s two biggest theater chains, AMC Entertainment and Regal Cinemas, Bloomberg reported. That would guarantee exclusive 45-day theatrical windows and a moratorium on distributing the movies on streaming services for at least 90 days, with potentially financial penalties if Paramount failed to hold up its end of the bargain. It’s worth noting that the CEOs of AMC and Regal have come out strongly in support of the Paramount-WBD merger.

	Paramount has publicly stated that it’s willing to put the 30-movie commitment into writing. That’s designed to counter the allegation in the antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 state attorneys general that a merged Paramount-Warner Bros. would have excessive control over the market for theatrical releases. The idea seems to be that it would serve as a guardrail against Paramount-WBD hoarding its studio output for the benefit of its own Paramount+ and HBO Max streamers. A trial in the case is slated to start in March 2027. Ellison is under pressure to find an out-of-court settlement with the states before then. But it’s unclear whether the 30-title/45-day window guarantee would be an acceptable concession for the state AGs. Meanwhile, it doesn’t address another key allegation in the states’ lawsuit: that Paramount-WBD would have excessive power in the U.S. market for basic cable TV.
	

	But the bottom-line question is this: What if most of these promised 30 movies are duds or just small-draw specialty titles?

	In a New York Times op-ed last week, Ellison admitted he can’t guarantee the financial performance of a particular theatrical movie release. What he is willing to stand behind is a vow to take more shots on goal.

	“In my career, ‘G.I. Joe: Retaliation’ met financial expectations, ‘Top Gun: Maverick’ exceeded them, and ‘Terminator: Dark Fate’ fell short. I am proud of all these films, but nobody can dictate what audiences will love,” he wrote. “What I can promise is the work, and more of it.”

	But higher studio output in terms of the number of titles doesn’t correlate with a bigger payoff for the industry (or Paramount-WBD itself). In focusing on quantity, Ellison is glossing over the question of actual financial returns.

	You don’t have to take my word for the fact that a bigger slate doesn’t necessarily translate into more revenue. Paramount has acknowledged it.

	Paramount’s 2025 film slate nearly doubled from eight films in 2025 to 15 this year. This year, Paramount has told Wall Street it expects “significantly lower theatrical revenue year-over-year due to lower average box office revenue per film across more releases.” A big reason is a tough year-over-year comparison because of Tom Cruise’s “Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning” blockbuster in 2025, which took in almost $600 million at the global box office.

	In the second quarter of 2026, Paramount Pictures’ theatrical revenue plummeted 45%, to $138 million (again, largely because of the comparison to the year-earlier period that included “Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning”). Its biggest theatrical release in the quarter was “Scary Movie,” which has grossed $108 million domestically (and $231 million worldwide) since its June 5 release date.

	For now, Paramount isn’t producing the billion-dollar box office smashes that drive millions of butts into theater seats (not to mention robust sales of novelty popcorn buckets). There’s nothing from the studio that is close to rivaling, say, the 2026 successes of Disney-Pixar’s “Toy Story 5,” Universal’s “The Odyssey” from Christopher Nolan, Sony’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” or Lionsgate’s “Michael.” To be sure, Warner’s “Dune 3” releasing in December 2026 could be a billion-dollar hit but unless the merger unexpectedly closes before then, that’s not part of a Paramount-WBD lineup.
	

	One Paramount Q2 movie release that wasn’t called out by the company in its quarterly filing: 3D concert film “Billie Eilish: Hit Me Hard and Soft,” directed by Eilish and James Cameron. (That’s Ellison pictured above at the L.A. premiere of the movie at Village Theatre on May 6.) It grossed $9.9 million domestically over a two-week theatrical run in May. The film got rave reviews, with a 91% Rotten Tomatoes critics’ score, and was undoubtedly enjoyed by many fans.

	But stringing together a bunch of sub-$10 million movie releases isn’t going to turn things around for movie theaters in America.

schema.headline: David Ellison Is Promising Theater Owners Contractual Guarantees for Paramount-Warner Bros. 30-Film Annual Slate. But What if Moviegoers Don’t Care?

	Whitney Houston is ready to dance with somebody — in Barbieland.

	Mattel is honoring the late pop icon with a new Barbie Signature doll inspired by Houston’s colorful look from the 1987 music video for “I Wanna Dance With Somebody (Who Loves Me).” The $60 collectible launches Aug. 8 at Target stores and online at Amazon, Walmart, Target and Mattel Creations.

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

										OFFICIAL RELEASE						

					Whitney Houston Barbie		

		
	

	The doll recreates Houston’s instantly recognizable ensemble from the video, complete with a purple tank dress, colorful drop earrings and bright eye makeup. Naturally, she also comes performance-ready with her own microphone stand.
	

	Houston’s estate worked closely with Mattel on the collectible. Pat Houston, executor of the Estate of Whitney E. Houston and president of the Whitney E. Houston Legacy Foundation, collaborated with the Barbie design team alongside Primary Wave Music, weighing in on everything from the doll’s wardrobe to the singer’s signature glam.

	The Whitney Houston Barbie will make its official debut Saturday at the fifth annual Legacy of Love Gala in Atlanta, an event hosted by the Whitney E. Houston Legacy Foundation. Its arrival comes as Houston’s estate continues to celebrate more than four decades since the singer first emerged as one of pop music’s most formidable voices.

	Released as the lead single from Houston’s sophomore album, “Whitney,” “I Wanna Dance With Somebody” became one of the singer’s defining hits and earned her the Grammy for best female pop vocal performance in 1988. The album itself made history as the first by a female artist to debut at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, while the song was part of Houston’s still-unmatched run of seven consecutive No. 1 singles.
	

	The new release joins Barbie Signature’s growing roster of dolls modeled after musicians and cultural icons, which has previously included Tina Turner, Stevie Nicks, Gloria Estefan and Mariah Carey. 

	Shop the Whitney Houston Barbie here.

title: Mahesh Babu’s Look in S.S. Rajamouli’s ‘Varanasi’ Unveiled
description: Two new character stills of Mahesh Babu from S.S. Rajamouli‘s “Varanasi” were released Sunday to mark the actor’s birthday, showing his character Ru
body:
Two new character stills of Mahesh Babu from S.S. Rajamouli‘s “Varanasi” were released Sunday to mark the actor’s birthday, showing his character Rudhra on location in Africa.

	The film’s story spans thousands of years and traverses multiple continents, with locations ranging from Antarctica to Africa to the titular Indian city. Babu plays the dual roles of the protagonist Rudhra and Hindu God Rama, Priyanka Chopra Jonas plays a character named Mandakini and the main antagonist Kumbha is played by Prithviraj Sukumaran.
	

	The images were shot at the Kilimanjaro and Maasai Mara locations, two of the African settings featured in the film. In one still, Mahesh Babu reclines on a bamboo raft in a jungle setting, dressed in a loose olive-toned shirt and dark cargo trousers, with tousled curly hair and a full beard. The other image shows him in profile against the African savannah, with giraffes and zebras visible in the background.




	

					Mahesh Babu – “Varanasi”
									Sri Durga Arts/Showing Business
	



	Rajamouli described the character’s dual nature in a note accompanying the stills. “Rudhra was born to fulfil a purpose much larger than himself. He carries a destiny he did not ask for. He is witty, he is vulnerable, and he is fierce. That is what Mahesh brought to him. Anyone can play fierce. Very few can play fierce and fragile in the same breath,” he said in an Instagram post.

	The director also reflected on the Africa shoot itself. “These frames are from our Africa schedule, and the land gave us something no set could. Shooting around Kilimanjaro and in the Masai Mara, I was stunned. There were mornings I felt even the 1.43:1 Imax frame could not hold what was in front of us,” he said.
	

	The stills mark the latest in a series of character reveals from the production, following images of Priyanka Chopra Jonas released for her birthday.

	Babu, who spent a year preparing for the role, underwent three months of Kalari martial arts training solely to adjust his posture for the character’s period-appropriate bearing. “I’m playing Lord Rama’s character, it required posture… you can’t stand like modern characters,” he has said to Variety.

	He also trained with a track and field team for several months to modify his running style. “When I saw the shot, I was really happy. It was worth it, because that six months of training for that one shot was really worth it,” he said. “The way I walked changed, the way I stood changed, everything changed.”

	“Varanasi” is Rajamouli’s follow-up to the Academy Award-winning “RRR.” M.M. Keeravani, who won the Oscar for “RRR’s” “Naatu Naatu,” is returning to score the new film.“Varanasi” opens in theaters worldwide on April 7, 2027.

title: Protest at the Locarno Film Festival Remembers 60,000 Names of the Dead of Gaza
description:
Locarno became the latest film festival to see protests at the continuing situation in Gaza and Palestine‘s Occupied Territories. 

	While music fro
body:
Locarno became the latest film festival to see protests at the continuing situation in Gaza and Palestine‘s Occupied Territories. 

	While music from the Campari Lounge boomed into the evening, approximately 100 demonstrators unwound a shroud bearing the names of 60,000 people who have been killed in Gaza since the beginning of the war two and a half years ago.

	One of the organizers, Dr. Michele Ghielmini from Swiss Healthcare Workers Against Genocide, told Variety that the protestors were not aligned to any political party and were not attempting to disrupt the festival. The location and time of the protest had been agreed with the festival organizers and the police. 
	



	

									Credit: John Bleasdale
	



	The banner containing the 60,000 names had previously been displayed in Amsterdam and in front of the Swiss Parliament in Bern. 


	Ghielmini said: “The festival is an opportunity because a lot of people are here, a lot of people from all over the world, but also importantly, a lot of people from Switzerland. Not all people of Switzerland have been sensitive in the same way to these actions of the Swiss government, and in particular, the German part of Switzerland was less sensitive. The Italian and French-speaking parts were more sensitive to it, and because of the film festival, there are more people from the German part of Switzerland here. Also, more press from the German part of Switzerland, and because of that, we thought it would be a good moment again to call attention to what has happened and to what is still happening in Gaza.”

	According to literature the protestors distributed, they are calling on the Swiss government to pressure Israel to open the borders of Gaza to relief organizations and the media, as well as to allow for injured civilians of Gaza to receive medical treatment in Switzerland. They also demand that the Swiss government impose sanctions if the Israelis continue to violate the Geneva convention. 
	

	The festival has been relatively untouched by the kind of political controversy which dogged the Berlin Film Festival earlier this year. There are films in competition from Palestinian filmmakers, such as Mohanad Yaqubi’s feature-length documentary “Revolutionaries Never Die,” in the Concorso Cineasti del Presente (Filmmakers of the Present) competition, and Palestinian-Jordanian director Asmahan Bkerat’s debut feature “Concrete Land” in the Semaine de la Critique section. Israeli producers are participating in some industry events.

	“The festival was informed in advance that a protest was being planned,” fest organizers told Variety. “As with any peaceful demonstration, we respect people’s right to free speech and to express their views, provided it takes place safely and without disrupting other attendees.”

	Over 8,000 attendees crammed into the Grand Piazza an hour after the protest had peacefully concluded for a sold-out screening of Olivia Wilde’s “The Invite.”

schema.headline: Protest at the Locarno Film Festival Remembers 60,000 Names of the Dead of Gaza

title: Locarno Sufi Trance Doc ‘As Light as Air’ Director Umair Bilal on Surrendering to a Pakistani Shrine Town: ‘I Became Part of Its Rhythm’
description:
Umair Bilal spent months in Sehwan, Pakistan, trying to direct a documentary. Then he gave up.

	“Every time I tried to impose that logic onto Sehwa
body:
Umair Bilal spent months in Sehwan, Pakistan, trying to direct a documentary. Then he gave up.

	“Every time I tried to impose that logic onto Sehwan, it felt like I was working against the place rather than with it,” the Pakistani filmmaker tells Variety of his debut feature, “As Light as Air,” which premieres in Semaine de la Critique at the 79th Locarno Film Festival. What began as an attempt to find characters and structure inside the Sufi shrine town instead became a 65-minute surrender to its rhythm – no plot, no protagonist, just pilgrims, malangs – wandering ascetics who have given up conventional life to devote themselves to the shrine – and the ecstatic communal trance of the dhamal.
	

	Bilal traces the project’s origins to sensory fragments rather than plot. “What stayed with me was not a sequence of events, but a series of sensations: people praying in deeply absorbed, almost transcendent states, the smell of burning incense, the glow of oil lamps, devotional music, and the feeling that these places operated according to a different logic from the outside world,” he says.


	Sehwan quickly overtook whatever nostalgia had drawn him there in the first place. “My childhood may have opened the door to Sehwan, but once I arrived, Sehwan gradually replaced those memories with its own reality,” he says. “By the end, I realized the emotional and visual world of the film belonged far more to Sehwan than to my childhood memories of it.”

	The shift from filmmaker to participant happened gradually, not in a single moment. Bilal describes an improvised method he developed with co-cinematographer Konstantin Stell: standing at intersections and asking which street was “calling” them, then following it without rationalizing the choice. “Quite often we would spend the next eight hours filming whatever unfolded there,” he says.
	

	That same instinct carried into the edit with editor Siddhant Sarin. “We began with an initial structure guided by emotion, letting images and sound dictate their own rhythm,” Bilal says. “Rather than simply watching people engage with spirituality, we wanted to reinterpret the footage so viewers could move closer to a feeling of immersion and journey through those emotions themselves.”

	“I was no longer standing outside Sehwan trying to explain it,” he says of the moment the project stopped feeling like a film he was making. “I had become part of its rhythm.”

	Bilal resists categorizing the film for audiences used to character-driven documentaries. “I don’t really pitch the film by saying, ‘It’s an experimental documentary.’ I think labels can sometimes create unnecessary distance,” he says. He compares its structure to music rather than plot. “It moves through repetition, variation, tension, release, and emotional progression rather than cause and effect. The film asks audiences to inhabit a place instead of constantly asking, ‘What happens next?’”

	The post-production team spans Berlin and Mumbai – composer Sui Sofie Heinz and post-production supervisor Philipp Schmeelcke in Berlin, sound designer Sudarshan Sawant and colorist Mahak Gupta in Mumbai – alongside Sarin’s editing. Bilal says the international makeup wasn’t a plan. “I didn’t consciously set out to build an international team. Looking back, that is what it became, but it was never a strategy,” he says. “None of the collaborations felt strictly professional or transactional. They developed through friendship and long conversations about life, cinema, and how we understood the material.”

	Heinz began composing only after immersing herself in raw footage and long conversations with Bilal about his years in Sehwan. “We never wanted there to be a clear boundary between the field recordings and the score,” he says. “We wanted the music and the recorded sounds to flow into one another so naturally that the audience would stop thinking about where one ended and the other began.”

	On the ethics of filming a spiritual community that isn’t his own, Bilal describes weeks spent without a camera – sitting with pilgrims, shoe-keepers and flower sellers before ever shooting. “I have my own relationship with Sufism, but I would never claim the experiences of the malangs or pilgrims as my own,” he says. “The relationship had to exist before the film. The camera came after the human connection, not before it.”
	

	One remark stuck with him: a Malang once suggested it was Qalandar, not Bilal, who had called him to Sehwan. “A Malang said that to me very early on, and I found it interesting because it reflected how many people in Sehwan understand their relationship to the shrine and spiritual nature of the city,” Bilal says. “It reminded me that the film wasn’t simply the product of my own intentions.”

	The film also makes a deliberate omission: it never directly addresses the 2017 ISIS suicide bombing at the Lal Shahbaz Qalandar shrine. “The bombing is part of Sehwan’s history, but I didn’t want it to become the lens through which audiences understood Sehwan,” Bilal says. “I tried to ask a different question: where does Sehwan’s resilience come from?”

	Asked about Pakistan’s place in his identity as a filmmaker based between Abu Dhabi and Berlin, Bilal points to lineage rather than distance. He names Dziga Vertov, Mani Kaul and Gianfranco Rosi as touchstones. “I don’t think of them as influences to imitate. I think of them as filmmakers I continue to learn from,” he says. “If ‘As Light as Air’ adds even a small voice to that ongoing conversation, I would feel incredibly fortunate.”

            Never-before-seen photos are shedding new light on Liam Payne's final hours ... showing the singer inside his Buenos Aires hotel before his fatal fall.
      
    
            Daily Mail obtained more than 3,000 documents and photos from the police investigation into the late One Direction singer's October 2024 death ... including images showing him drinking, interacting with two sex workers and moving around the CasaSur Palermo Hotel.
      
    
            One photo reportedly shows Liam swinging around a pole the night before his death. Others show hotel workers bringing booze to his room and Liam meeting the two women in the lobby the following day.
      

            The women allegedly told investigators Liam sang for them and asked about getting cocaine ... with the report also claiming he wanted help making crack.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... prosecutors said Liam spent his final day drinking heavily, hiring two prostitutes and doing cocaine before hotel employees carried him from the lobby back to his room.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We later reported the 31-year-old appeared to be trying to escape the hotel when he fell from his third-floor balcony. A hotel employee had called 911 shortly before the fall ... expressing concern he could hurt himself because his room had a balcony.
      
    
            Toxicology testing later showed cocaine, crack, ketamine and alcohol in his system.

            Two people died -- including a 5-month-old girl -- and 12 others plunged into the waters near NYC's Statue of Liberty after their boat capsized Saturday night, according to law enforcement.
      
    
            NYPD sources tell TMZ ... the terrifying incident occurred off the coast of Liberty Island in New York Harbor, where the world famous monument stands ... 14 people were on the boat that suddenly overturned, causing them to be thrown into the choppy waters.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Our sources say NYPD Aviation and Harbor Units quickly responded, along with a scuba diving team, after receiving a call for an overturned vessel.
      

            We're told a 27-year-old woman and a 5-month-old girl were pulled from the bay in critical condition. Our sources say the two were later pronounced dead at a hospital in Brooklyn.
      
    
            The good news is ... NYPD rescued the other 12 people from the bay, and they were taken to a local hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
      
    
            As for how this happened ... our sources say it's not clear just yet, but the investigation is ongoing.
